content: Intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), also referred to as intrauterine growth restriction, describes a condition where a fetus does not grow at the expected rate during pregnancy. Classification: 1. Asymmetrical IUGR: This is the more common type. In this form, fetal weight is restricted first, followed by length, while the head continues to grow at a normal or near-normal rate (a phenomenon known as head sparing). This head sparing mechanism is thought to be an evolutionary adaptation to prioritize brain development. Asymmetrical IUGR is typically caused by external factors affecting the fetus during the later stages of pregnancy. 2. Symmetrical IUGR: This is less common but more concerning. It usually begins early in gestation. Since most neurons are formed by the 18th week of gestation, fetuses with symmetrical IUGR are at a higher risk of permanent neurological deficits. Pathophysiology: When the cause of IUGR is external to the fetus (e.g., maternal or uteroplacental factors), the transfer of oxygen and nutrients to the fetus is reduced. This results in decreased fetal glycogen and lipid stores, often leading to hypoglycemia at birth. Chronic hypoxemia can stimulate increased erythropoietin production, resulting in polycythemia. Other complications include hypothermia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, hypocalcemia, and pulmonary hemorrhage. If the cause of IUGR is intrinsic to the fetus, such as genetic abnormalities or infections, growth restriction occurs due to these underlying factors. Causes: Life-Threatening Causes: Alcohol abuse Cardiovascular disease Chronic hypertension Drug addiction Kidney failure Pulmonary disease Sickle-cell disease Syphilis Toxoplasmosis Tuberculosis Common Causes: Abnormal umbilical cord insertion Chronic placental abruption Placental insufficiency Maternal malnutrition Maternal smoking Gestational hypertension Multiple pregnancies Vertical transmission of infections Epidemiology: At least 60% of the 4 million neonatal deaths worldwide each year are associated with low birth weight, which is often caused by IUGR, preterm delivery, or genetic/chromosomal abnormalities. This highlights the significant impact of under-nutrition as a major health issue at birth. Risk Factors: Maternal risk factors contributing to IUGR include: Alcohol abuse Smoking Drug addiction Poor nutrition High blood pressure or cardiovascular disease Kidney disease Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis: Post-delivery growth and development depend on the severity and cause of IUGR. IUGR increases the risk of pregnancy and neonatal complications, including non-reassuring fetal heart rates during labor, often necessitating cesarean delivery. Perinatal mortality rates are 4-8 times higher in infants with IUGR, and 50% of surviving infants experience morbidity. History and Symptoms: Pregnant women may notice that their baby is not growing as expected. Physical Examination: Uterine fundal height is often smaller than expected for the baby’s gestational age.
